    for candidate in ([full, url] if full != url else [url]):
        try:

            ext = os.path.splitext(candidate)[1] or ".jpg"
            n = save(os.path.join(OUT, name + ext), data)

            break

print()

for name, url in PAGES:

        data = get(url)
        n = save(os.path.join(OUT, name + ".html"), data)
        print(f"OK   {name}.html  {n:>9,} bytes")

# Rob Gray's free infographics — local copies

**Saved 2026-09-03** from [perceptionaction.com](https://perceptionaction.com/), index page
[/resources/](https://perceptionaction.com/resources/).

`NOTES.md` said to take local copies because it is one person's website and the material is
free but not archived anywhere else. This is that.

**All images are the full-resolution originals**, not the 1024px versions the site displays.
The `-1024x576` suffix WordPress appends was stripped to reach the source file.

## What is here

| File | What it is | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| `comparative-training-studies.md` | **21 head-to-head training studies**, traditional vs ecological, extracted to a searchable table | **The page Joe brings when someone pushes back.** Evidence, not philosophy. |
| `two-approaches.md` + `.jpg` | Information-processing vs ecological, side by side. Transcribed from the image. | Lets Joe state the view he disagrees with, fairly. See the note on the last row. |
| `cla.jpg` | Constraints-Led Approach infographic | The core diagram of the whole course. |
| `sports-injury.jpg` | Ecological approach to sports injury | **The most on-mission of the images** — injury is the workspace's whole subject. |
| `differential-learning.jpg` | Differential Learning | Background. DL is not the CLA; keep them distinct. |
| `variability-of-practice.jpg` | Variability of Practice | Feeds the "no single correct technique" argument. |
| `direct-learning.jpg` | Direct Learning | Background theory. |
| `*.html` | The source pages as served | Kept so the extractions can be re-checked against the original. |

## Two rows worth pulling into lesson 0001

Both land on the opposed/unopposed argument from independent directions:

- **`two-approaches.md`, last row** — *Modularity / Separability / Decomposition* versus
  *Coupling / Inseparability / Simplification*. Removing the defender is decomposition. The
  ecological claim is that you cannot take perception and action apart.
- **`comparative-training-studies.md`, study 17** — Caldeira et al. (2023), volleyball.
  **Task simplification beat task decomposition** in a head-to-head. That is the exact
  distinction, tested, with a result.

Also note **studies 9 and 18** (Orangi et al., 2021a and 2023): both CLA and DL lowered ACL
injury risk factors, with larger effects for CLA. **Those are the two rows a physician will
care about.**

## Handling

Gray's material, free and public, saved here for internal study only. **Do not republish
and do not commit.** When a claim from these goes into a lesson, cite the underlying study —
not the infographic and not this folder.

## Re-fetching

The script that built this folder is disposable and lives in the job tmp dir. To rebuild:
download each page listed on [/resources/](https://perceptionaction.com/resources/), strip
the `-NNNxNNN` suffix from image URLs to get the original, and re-extract the tables.
Watch for two traps found on 2026-09-03:

1. The site's WordPress **calendar widget is a `<table>`** and gets scraped as content.
2. The Two Approaches graphic is listed on `/resources/` next to the terminology video, so
   it is easy to mislabel as that video's thumbnail. **It is not.** It is the infographic.

# RTP_Constraints_Course

A **teaching workspace**, not a code project. It runs on Matt Pocock's `teach` skill
(mattpocock-skills 1.2.3).

**Learner:** Joe Smith, assistant athletic trainer, Baylor Athletics.
**Sponsor:** Eric Rash.
**Topic:** ecological dynamics and the constraints-led approach (CLA) applied to the last
phase of return to performance in American football.

## How to work here

Type `/teach` in this directory. Do not hand-roll lessons — the skill owns the workflow.
`teach` and `ask-matt` are `disable-model-invocation: true`, so **a human must type the
slash command**; the agent cannot invoke them.

Read before doing anything: `MISSION.md`, then `NOTES.md` (open questions and framing
wrinkles), then `RESOURCES.md`.

## Layout

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `MISSION.md` | Why Joe is learning this. Grounds every teaching decision. |
| `INTERVIEW.md` | **Mission interview to run with Joe. Do this before lesson 0001.** 45 min; Parts 1 and 2 are the ones that matter. Run 2026-09-03. |
| `interviews/` | Transcripts of interviews actually run, plus a key-answers digest. Joe's mission interview lives here. **Names athletes and their injuries — never commit, never paste into an artifact or an external service.** |
| `RESOURCES.md` | Curated trusted sources. Most are already in Eric's SecondBrain library. |
| `NOTES.md` | Open questions, preferences, working notes. |
| `assets/` | Reusable lesson components. `course.css` is shared by every lesson. |
| `lessons/` | `NNNN-slug.html` — the unit of teaching. None written yet. |
| `reference/` | `*.html` cheat sheets. The compressed residue of lessons. |
| `sources/` | Full-text books and long PDFs obtained legitimately. Author-supplied — **never redistribute, never commit.** |
| `docs/handoffs/` | Durable cross-session handoffs. Newest first. |
| `learning-records/` | `NNNN-slug.md` ADR-style records. Created lazily at the first record. |

## Rules specific to this workspace

- **Ground in `RESOURCES.md`, never in parametric knowledge.** This field has a lot of
  confident bad writing in it. Cite everything.
- **Football examples only.** Generic team-sport examples will not land with position coaches.
- **Every lesson ends in something Joe could do at practice tomorrow.**
- `GLOSSARY.md` does not exist yet by design — see `NOTES.md`.
- **Phase 2 is a drill-design tool.** Do not start it until the lessons have specified it.
  Route: `/grill-with-docs` → `/prototype` → `/implement`. Local-only per Baylor IT.

## Source library

Papers referenced as `LIB/…` live in `~/SecondBrain/Knowledge/library/research-papers/`.
Search with `memsearch search "<query>" --top-k 5`. Zotero MCP was down on 2026-09-01.

import csv
import glob
import io
import os
import subprocess

D = "/Users/kristinarash/Downloads/vFlat/iPhone 15"
OUT = "/Users/kristinarash/.claude/jobs/2a119c54/tmp/scan_quality.csv"

files = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(D, "*.jpg")))
rows = []

for i, f in enumerate(files, 1):
    try:
        tsv = subprocess.run(
            ["tesseract", f, "stdout", "--psm", "1", "tsv"],
            capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=180,
        ).stdout
    except Exception as e:
        rows.append((os.path.basename(f), -1, 0, f"ERROR {e}"))
        continue

    confs, words = [], 0
    for r in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(tsv), delimiter="\t", quoting=csv.QUOTE_NONE):
        try:
            c = float(r.get("conf", -1))
        except (TypeError, ValueError):
            continue
        txt = (r.get("text") or "").strip()
        if c >= 0 and txt:
            confs.append(c)
            words += 1

    mean = sum(confs) / len(confs) if confs else 0
    rows.append((os.path.basename(f), round(mean, 1), words, ""))
    print(f"{i:>3}/{len(files)}  {mean:5.1f}  {words:>5} words  {os.path.basename(f)}", flush=True)

with open(OUT, "w", newline="") as fh:
    w = csv.writer(fh)
    w.writerow(["file", "mean_conf", "words", "note"])
    w.writerows(rows)

good = [r for r in rows if r[1] >= 85]
ok = [r for r in rows if 75 <= r[1] < 85]
bad = [r for r in rows if 0 <= r[1] < 75]

print()
print("=" * 60)
print(f"TOTAL PAGES : {len(rows)}")
print(f"GOOD  (>=85): {len(good)}")
print(f"OK  (75-85) : {len(ok)}")
print(f"POOR  (<75) : {len(bad)}")
tot_words = sum(r[2] for r in rows)
print(f"TOTAL WORDS : {tot_words:,}")
print()
print("WORST 12:")
for r in sorted([r for r in rows if r[1] >= 0], key=lambda r: r[1])[:12]:
    print(f"  {r[1]:5.1f}  {r[2]:>5} words  {r[0]}")
print()
print(f"csv -> {OUT}")

`~/Downloads/vFlat/iPhone 15/` — **`p014.jpg` through `p101.jpg`**, 88 files, no gaps, no duplicates.

OCR was not reliable enough — I tried three tuning passes and one made it worse. So I built contact sheets of just the folio strips and read all 88 by eye. Two independent methods then agreed on which six pages the re-shoots covered, which is what gave me confidence to rename.

I put a validation gate in front of the rename that aborted twice before I got it right. Worth it.

One command that replaces the manual end-of-day sequence: "any loose ends?" → "commit and push what needs to be" → "is this in memory?" → "write a handoff so Codex can pick this up."

---
name: book-scan-page-ordering
description: "Putting phone-scanned book pages in page order: OCR of the folio is unreliable, read a contact sheet instead; sort by mtime, never filename"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  modified: 2026-09-03
---

**Learned 2026-09-03** putting 88 vFlat iPhone scans of the Myszka football book into page
order. Cost several wasted OCR-tuning passes before the right method surfaced.

## Do not trust OCR for the page number

Three tuning attempts; **one made it worse** (80 of 88 unread). Two failure modes:

- A bottom-strip crop catches **body text and citation years**. Taking the longest digit
  token then picks a 4-digit year over a 2-digit folio.
- Tesseract **confuses 5 with 9**. It read page **50 as 90 with 8/8 unanimous votes** — a
  confident wrong answer, which is worse than an unread one. Vote counts do not rescue this.

## What actually works — read a contact sheet

1. Crop a tight band around the **centred** folio: `x 0.36–0.64`, `y 0.900–0.952` of the
   page image. Autocontrast, grayscale.
2. Tile ~44 of them into one PNG with the capture index labelled beside each.
3. **Look at it.** Two sheets covered 88 pages, unambiguously, in two passes.

Folios are large, bold and isolated — trivial to read by eye, and the thing OCR keeps
getting wrong. Do not keep tuning tesseract; switch methods after the second failure.

## Ordering traps

- **Sort by mtime, never by filename.** macOS appends ` (1)` on download collisions, and
  `…17-35-17 (1).jpg` sorts *before* `…17-35-17.jpg` while the timestamps say the reverse.
- **Same-second captures land out of page order.** Two pairs were swapped this way.
- A page shot out of sequence (67 before 66) looks exactly like a **missing page** if your
  sample happens to skip the tile it is on. Verify a "gap" before believing it.

## Other findings

- **A zero-word OCR page may just be blank.** One page returned no text and was genuinely
  blank in the book — but still carried a printed folio.
- **Bad pages cluster in time**, not randomly: all 7 poor scans fell inside one two-minute
  window. Re-shoot the window, not the whole book.
- **The scan folder is live** while the human is still working. Any script must re-verify
  its map rather than assert on a file count — a new shot broke an `assert` mid-analysis.
- Rename via a **temp prefix in two passes** so no collision is possible, and always write
  an old→new manifest so the rename is reversible.

## Quality bar that worked

vFlat Scan on iPhone, ~2000×3200 px (~360 DPI) — above the 300 DPI OCR target. Median
tesseract confidence **95.0**. Turn the app's OCR off, or just use
`ocrmypdf --force-ocr`, which discards any text layer the app added and makes the setting
irrelevant.

Pipeline: `img2pdf` (page order) → `ocrmypdf --force-ocr --rotate-pages --deskew` →
`ingest-book` at **full-text tier**.

**Learned 2026-09-03** putting 88 vFlat iPhone scans of the Myszka football book into page
order. Cost several wasted OCR-tuning passes before the right method surfaced.

## Do not trust OCR for the page number

Three tuning attempts; **one made it worse** (80 of 88 unread). Two failure modes:

- A bottom-strip crop catches **body text and citation years**. Taking the longest digit
  token then picks a 4-digit year over a 2-digit folio.
- Tesseract **confuses 5 with 9**. It read page **50 as 90 with 8/8 unanimous votes** — a
  confident wrong answer, which is worse than an unread one. Vote counts do not rescue this.

## What actually works — read a contact sheet

1. Crop a tight band around the **centred** folio: `x 0.36–0.64`, `y 0.900–0.952` of the
   page image. Autocontrast, grayscale.
2. Tile ~44 of them into one PNG with the capture index labelled beside each.
3. **Look at it.** Two sheets covered 88 pages, unambiguously, in two passes.

Folios are large, bold and isolated — trivial to read by eye, and the thing OCR keeps
getting wrong. Do not keep tuning tesseract; switch methods after the second failure.

## Ordering traps

- **Sort by mtime, never by filename.** macOS appends ` (1)` on download collisions, and
  `…17-35-17 (1).jpg` sorts *before* `…17-35-17.jpg` while the timestamps say the reverse.
- **Same-second captures land out of page order.** Two pairs were swapped this way.
- A page shot out of sequence (67 before 66) looks exactly like a **missing page** if your
  sample happens to skip the tile it is on. Verify a "gap" before believing it.

## Other findings

- **A zero-word OCR page may just be blank.** One page returned no text and was genuinely
  blank in the book — but still carried a printed folio.
- **Bad pages cluster in time**, not randomly: all 7 poor scans fell inside one two-minute
  window. Re-shoot the window, not the whole book.
- **The scan folder is live** while the human is still working. Any script must re-verify
  its map rather than assert on a file count — a new shot broke an `assert` mid-analysis.
- Rename via a **temp prefix in two passes** so no collision is possible, and always write
  an old→new manifest so the rename is reversible.

## Quality bar that worked

vFlat Scan on iPhone, ~2000×3200 px (~360 DPI) — above the 300 DPI OCR target. Median
tesseract confidence **95.0**. Turn the app's OCR off, or just use
`ocrmypdf --force-ocr`, which discards any text layer the app added and makes the setting
irrelevant.

Pipeline: `img2pdf` (page order) → `ocrmypdf --force-ocr --rotate-pages --deskew` →
`ingest-book` at **full-text tier**.

**Key Exchanges:**
- Asked for the fast way to open a new terminal window with tmux in VS Code. Answer: `Ctrl+b` then `c` — but VS Code intercepts `Ctrl+b` for sidebar toggle before tmux receives it.
- Two options presented: (A) tell VS Code to skip the binding, or (B) remap the tmux prefix to `Ctrl+a` in `~/.tmux.conf`.

**Decisions Made:**
- Chose option A — added `"terminal.integrated.commandsToSkipShell": ["-workbench.action.toggleSidebarVisibility"]` to VS Code `settings.json`. Rationale: one-line change, keeps the default tmux prefix so online tmux docs/guides match his keys without translation.

### Session (07:31)

**Context:** Setting up faster tmux window creation inside the VS Code integrated terminal on macOS.

**Key Exchanges:**
- Asked for the fast way to open a new terminal window with tmux in VS Code. Answer: `Ctrl+b` then `c` — but VS Code intercepts `Ctrl+b` for sidebar toggle before tmux receives it.
- Two options presented: (A) tell VS Code to skip the binding, or (B) remap the tmux prefix to `Ctrl+a` in `~/.tmux.conf`.

**Decisions Made:**
- Chose option A — added `"terminal.integrated.commandsToSkipShell": ["-workbench.action.toggleSidebarVisibility"]` to VS Code `settings.json`. Rationale: one-line change, keeps the default tmux prefix so online tmux docs/guides match his keys without translation.

**Lessons Learned:**
- VS Code's `terminal.integrated.commandsToSkipShell` accepts a `-` prefix on a command ID to *remove* it from the skip list, letting the keystroke pass through to the shell/tmux instead of being consumed by the editor.
- The `Ctrl+b` collision between tmux prefix and VS Code sidebar toggle is the standard gotcha when running tmux in the integrated terminal.
- No VS Code restart needed; the setting applies immediately.

**Files Changed:**
